lessonTitle: Common Surgical Ward Problems: Postoperative Complications and Fluid Balance

blocks.text: At 04:00 the nurse bleeps the surgical team: 'Mr S in bed 12 has passed only 40 mL of urine since midnight, his heart rate has crept up and he says his tummy feels tight.' He had emergency surgery yesterday. Three separate ward problems, oliguria, tachycardia and distension, may be one diagnosis or three, and the next 30 minutes decide which.

blocks.markdown: **Pain and nausea after surgery.** Uncontrolled pain delays mobilisation, impairs breathing and raises the risk of chest infection and thromboembolism. Use **multimodal analgesia**: regular simple analgesics (for example paracetamol), an anti-inflammatory where renal function, bleeding risk and the surgeon allow, regional or local techniques where appropriate, and titrated opioids for severe pain, with a pain score and sedation score recorded. Opioids cause nausea, sedation, respiratory depression, constipation and ileus. Postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV) is more likely in women, non-smokers, people with a history of PONV or motion sickness, and with postoperative opioids. Check the cause first (opioids, ileus, obstruction, uraemia, pain, infection); choose an antiemetic according to the cause, and avoid a prokinetic such as metoclopramide in suspected mechanical obstruction or perforation. All doses must be checked against current BNF and local guidance.

rows: Postoperative pain
Surgery, wound, inadequate analgesia, complication (collection, leak, ischaemia)
Assess score and examine; give regular multimodal analgesia; ask if the pain has changed in character
New severe or rising pain is a red flag for a complication, not just an analgesia problem
Nausea and vomiting
Opioids, anaesthesia, ileus, obstruction, uraemia, electrolyte disturbance
Review drugs, check abdomen and electrolytes, antiemetic matched to cause
Avoid prokinetics in suspected mechanical obstruction
Ileus
Bowel handling, opioids, low potassium or magnesium, sepsis, leak
Correct electrolytes, minimise opioids, mobilise, fluids, nasogastric decompression if vomiting
Exclude mechanical obstruction and anastomotic leak if it persists or the patient is unwell
Low urine output
Hypovolaemia or bleeding, sepsis, drugs, kidney injury, blocked catheter, retention
Check catheter, bladder scan, assess volume status, trends and bloods
Do not assume that fluid is the answer without assessing the patient
blocks.caption: Common postoperative ward problems with first actions.

blocks.markdown: **Fluids and urine output.** Urine output is a bedside marker of organ perfusion. A sustained output below about 0.5 mL/kg/h is a widely used trigger for assessment (check current KDIGO and local criteria). First check the catheter is draining (not kinked, blocked or displaced), then assess volume status (pulse, blood pressure, capillary refill, jugular venous pressure, fluid balance chart, wound and drain losses) and look for bleeding or sepsis. If the patient is hypovolaemic, give a measured crystalloid bolus according to local protocol and reassess after each bolus; avoid overload in those with heart or renal disease. Maintenance fluids for adults who cannot take enough orally are commonly 25 to 30 mL/kg/day of water, with potassium, sodium, chloride and glucose adjusted to need (follow current NICE and local fluid guidance).

blocks.caption: These are bedside screening calculations; individualise fluid prescriptions to the patient and reassess regularly.

blocks.title: Worked example 1: low urine output the night after emergency surgery
blocks.prompt: Mr S, 54, is 18 hours after emergency repair of a perforated duodenal ulcer. He weighs 78 kg and has a urinary catheter. Urine output has been 40 mL over the last 4 hours. Heart rate 112/min, blood pressure 98/60 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, temperature 37.9 C, capillary refill 3 seconds, abdomen soft but diffusely tender. Assess and plan.

steps.text: Quantify: 40 mL / 4 h / 78 kg = 0.13 mL/kg/h, well below the 0.5 mL/kg/h screening level. This is oliguria and needs an assessment, not a reassurance.

Check the cause in order: is the catheter draining (flush or reposition; bladder scan if no catheter)? It is. Is he hypovolaemic? Tachycardia, low-normal blood pressure and slow capillary refill suggest yes, from third-space losses, bleeding or sepsis after perforation.

Act: assess ABCDE, give oxygen if hypoxic, give a crystalloid bolus according to local protocol and reassess response, send blood tests (FBC, urea and electrolytes, lactate, CRP, group and save), review drugs that affect the kidney (for example NSAIDs), examine the wound and drains for bleeding or leak. Escalate to the registrar because the combination of tachycardia, hypotension tendency and oliguria suggests ongoing sepsis or bleeding.

Set a review: repeat the observations and urine output hourly; if there is no improvement after the fluid bolus, consider critical care review. Doses and regimens must be checked against current guidance.

blocks.answer: Oliguria at 0.13 mL/kg/h with signs of hypovolaemia: check the catheter, resuscitate with measured fluid boluses, investigate for sepsis or bleeding, escalate and review within the hour.

blocks.markdown: **Abdominal distension.** After surgery, distension can be caused by ileus, mechanical obstruction (adhesions, hernia, stoma problems), anastomotic leak with peritonitis, urinary retention, haemoperitoneum, ascites or simply swallowed air. Assess the patient first (ABCDE and vital signs, hydration, pain, vomiting, flatus and bowel opening, stoma output), then the abdomen: inspect for distension, scars and hernias; palpate for tenderness, guarding and a palpable bladder; percuss (tympanic note suggests gas; dullness suggests fluid or a full bladder); auscultate; examine the wound, stoma and drains; do a rectal examination if appropriate. Request bloods (urea and electrolytes including potassium and magnesium, FBC, CRP, lactate), a bladder scan when retention is possible, and imaging (abdominal X-ray or CT) when obstruction, leak or collection is suspected.

rows: Paralytic ileus
Diffuse distension, few or absent bowel sounds, vomiting, no pain beyond mild; electrolyte disturbance or opioids
Electrolytes; X-ray or CT showing gas throughout bowel
Correct causes, minimise opioids, decompress if vomiting, mobilise
Mechanical obstruction
Colicky pain, vomiting, tinkling bowel sounds, previous surgery or hernia
CT with transition point
Nil by mouth, fluids, decompression, surgical review
Anastomotic leak or peritonitis
Day 3 to 7 after bowel surgery, fever, tachycardia, worsening pain, rising CRP
CT with contrast
Resuscitate, antibiotics per local protocol, urgent senior surgical review
Urinary retention
Suprapubic discomfort and dullness, no urine
Bladder scan
Catheterise, record volume, observe for diuresis
blocks.caption: Differential diagnosis of postoperative distension.

blocks.title: Worked example 2: distension 36 hours after an incisional hernia repair
blocks.prompt: Mr T, 72, is 36 hours after open repair of an incisional hernia. He has vomited twice and says he has not passed wind. He takes oxycodone for pain. Observations are normal, the abdomen is distended but soft, with mild generalised discomfort and no guarding, and there are sparse bowel sounds. Potassium is 3.1 mmol/L and magnesium 0.5 mmol/L. Assess and plan.

steps.text: Formulate the problem: distension with vomiting and no flatus, most consistent with postoperative ileus (soft abdomen, normal observations, sparse bowel sounds, opioids, low potassium and low magnesium). The dangerous alternatives are mechanical obstruction at the hernia site, strangulation and an unrecognised complication, so they must be excluded.

Assess further: examine the hernia repair wound for tenderness, redness and irreducible swelling; check the bladder and stoma if present; review the fluid balance chart; get a lactate and venous gas. If pain is severe or lactate is raised, obtain a CT scan urgently and involve the senior.

Treat the causes: replace potassium and magnesium following local protocols (intravenous replacement doses and rates must be checked against the BNF and local guidance and ECG monitoring considered for hypokalaemia), review opioids and use non-opioid analgesia, encourage mobilisation, keep him nil by mouth or on sips, give maintenance fluids, and place a nasogastric tube if vomiting continues.
Review at a defined time: repeat observations and the abdominal examination at least every few hours; escalate if pain, tenderness, fever, tachycardia, rising lactate or worsening distension develop.

blocks.answer: Probable postoperative ileus caused by opioids and electrolyte disturbance: correct potassium and magnesium, reduce opioids, decompress if vomiting, and monitor for features of obstruction or leak, with explicit escalation triggers.

blocks.markdown: **Wound, anastomotic and thromboembolic complications.** *Surgical site infection* usually presents days 5 to 7 with pain, erythema, warmth, swelling, pus and fever: examine and swab the wound, open it if there is a collection and give antibiotics according to local guidance. *Wound dehiscence* may be heralded by a pink serous discharge and presents with a gaping wound; if bowel is visible (evisceration), cover with saline-soaked gauze, keep the patient nil by mouth, obtain intravenous access, call the senior surgeon and prepare for theatre. *Anastomotic leak* typically presents between days 3 and 7 with fever, tachycardia, ileus, worsening abdominal pain and rising inflammatory markers and requires urgent resuscitation, imaging and senior review. *Venous thromboembolism*: deep vein thrombosis presents with unilateral leg swelling, pain and warmth; pulmonary embolism with sudden breathlessness, pleuritic pain, tachycardia, hypoxia or collapse. Prophylaxis (early mobilisation, stockings or intermittent compression and pharmacological prophylaxis decided by risk assessment) reduces but does not abolish the risk, so a high index of suspicion remains.

blocks.title: Escalate early
blocks.text: Fever, tachycardia, rising pain, ileus, falling urine output or new oxygen requirement after surgery may be the first signs of a leak, sepsis, bleeding or pulmonary embolism. Review the patient yourself, take the observations seriously and inform the registrar early; follow your hospital's escalation policy.

items: Assess pain with a score and ask whether it has changed; new severe pain is a complication until proved otherwise.
Treat the cause of nausea and avoid prokinetics in suspected mechanical obstruction.
Check the catheter and volume status first when urine output falls.
For distension, resuscitate, examine, check electrolytes and bladder, and image if suspicious.
Check all doses and regimens against current BNF and local guidance.

points: Multimodal analgesia limits opioid side effects such as nausea, sedation and ileus, but new severe pain should prompt a search for a complication.
Oliguria is assessed by checking the catheter and the volume status, treating the cause and escalating if there is no response.
Abdominal distension is approached by resuscitation, examination and targeted tests to distinguish ileus, obstruction, leak and retention.
Recognise wound infection and dehiscence, anastomotic leak and venous thromboembolism early and escalate promptly.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old woman has had a sigmoid colectomy 3 days ago and is vomiting with a distended abdomen. A colleague suggests metoclopramide. When should this drug be avoided?

options.text: When mechanical bowel obstruction or perforation is suspected
When the patient has a mild headache
When the patient is mobilising well
When the patient is on regular paracetamol

questions.correctOptionText: When mechanical bowel obstruction or perforation is suspected

distractorRationale.a: Correct: prokinetics increase peristalsis and can be harmful in mechanical obstruction or perforation.
distractorRationale.b: A headache is not a contraindication.
distractorRationale.c: Mobility has no effect on its use.
distractorRationale.d: No interaction with paracetamol is relevant.

questions.explanation: Metoclopramide stimulates gastrointestinal motility, so it should not be used when the bowel is obstructed or perforated. Always exclude those problems and check doses and cautions against current BNF and local guidance.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man is on day 2 after a laparotomy with a morphine PCA. His pain score is controlled but he is drowsy, nauseated and constipated and has not mobilised. Which change is most appropriate?

options.text: Add or optimise regular non-opioid analgesia (and a regional or local technique if available), reduce the opioid as pain allows, and encourage mobilisation
Increase the morphine dose further to deepen the analgesia
Stop all analgesia to reduce sedation
Give a prokinetic and continue the same opioid regime

questions.correctOptionText: Add or optimise regular non-opioid analgesia (and a regional or local technique if available), reduce the opioid as pain allows, and encourage mobilisation

distractorRationale.a: Correct: multimodal analgesia reduces opioid requirements and their side effects.
distractorRationale.b: More opioid would worsen sedation, nausea and constipation.
distractorRationale.c: Stopping analgesia would cause pain, immobility and complications.
distractorRationale.d: Treats a symptom without addressing the cause and may be harmful if obstruction is present.

questions.explanation: Opioid side effects can be reduced by multimodal analgesia. Drugs and doses must be selected after considering renal function, bleeding risk and surgical advice, and checked against current guidance.

questions.stem: An 80 kg man with a urinary catheter has passed 100 mL of urine in the last 4 hours. Calculate his average urine output in mL/kg/h to two decimal places.
questions.explanation: Urine output = 100 mL / (4 h x 80 kg) = 0.31 mL/kg/h. This is below the commonly used 0.5 mL/kg/h screening level, so he needs assessment of the catheter, volume status and cause.

questions.stem: A 70 kg patient is nil by mouth after surgery and needs maintenance intravenous fluids. Using 25 mL/kg/day of water, calculate the daily maintenance water volume in mL.
questions.explanation: Volume = 25 mL/kg/day x 70 kg = 1750 mL per day. NICE guidance gives a range of 25 to 30 mL/kg/day, so the exact prescription must be individualised and checked against current guidance, taking account of ongoing losses, comorbidity and age.

questions.stem: A man 8 hours after a hernia repair has no catheter, lower abdominal discomfort, a distended lower abdomen with suprapubic dullness and has not passed urine for 10 hours. What is the most useful immediate step?

options.text: Perform a bladder scan and, if retention is confirmed, catheterise and record the volume
Order an urgent CT of the head
Give a prokinetic
Reassure and review in 24 hours

questions.correctOptionText: Perform a bladder scan and, if retention is confirmed, catheterise and record the volume

distractorRationale.a: Correct: suprapubic dullness and no urine suggest retention, which a bladder scan will confirm.
distractorRationale.c: A prokinetic does not treat urinary retention.
distractorRationale.d: A delay risks bladder overdistension and kidney injury.

questions.explanation: Urinary retention is a common cause of postoperative distension and discomfort. A bladder scan is a quick, non-invasive test, and catheterisation relieves the problem; record the volume drained and observe for post-obstructive diuresis.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old woman is on day 6 after a low anterior resection with primary anastomosis. She has a temperature of 38.2 C, a heart rate of 112/min, a respiratory rate of 22/min, blood pressure 104/62 mmHg, abdominal distension with generalised tenderness and vomiting. CRP has risen from 80 mg/L on day 3 to 250 mg/L. What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Treat as suspected anastomotic leak with sepsis: resuscitate, take cultures, give antibiotics per local sepsis protocol, arrange contrast CT and urgent senior surgical review
Diagnose ileus and give an antiemetic, reviewing in the morning
Start oral feeding to stimulate the bowel
Discharge with analgesia

questions.correctOptionText: Treat as suspected anastomotic leak with sepsis: resuscitate, take cultures, give antibiotics per local sepsis protocol, arrange contrast CT and urgent senior surgical review

distractorRationale.a: Correct: fever, tachycardia, distension, tenderness and a rising CRP on day 6 strongly suggest anastomotic leak, which needs urgent resuscitation, imaging and surgical review.
distractorRationale.b: Ileus does not explain the fever, tachycardia, tenderness and rising CRP.
distractorRationale.c: Oral feeding would be harmful with vomiting and suspected leak.

questions.explanation: The timing (days 3 to 7) and the combination of sepsis and peritoneal signs indicate leak until proved otherwise. Early recognition and escalation reduce mortality; drug and fluid choices must follow local guidance.

questions.stem: Because a patient is receiving prophylactic low molecular weight heparin, sudden breathlessness with tachycardia on day 5 after major abdominal surgery cannot be due to pulmonary embolism.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Prophylaxis reduces, but does not eliminate, the risk of thromboembolism. Sudden breathlessness with tachycardia after surgery must be assessed urgently for pulmonary embolism and other causes.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman is on day 5 after a right hemicolectomy. Her left calf is swollen, warm and tender with mild pitting oedema; observations are normal and she has no chest symptoms. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Suspect deep vein thrombosis: review thromboprophylaxis, arrange prompt diagnostic imaging (for example compression ultrasound) and start treatment per local guidance if imaging will be delayed
Massage the calf firmly to disperse the swelling
Encourage vigorous exercise and ignore the leg
Reassure that post-operative swelling is normal and review in a week

questions.correctOptionText: Suspect deep vein thrombosis: review thromboprophylaxis, arrange prompt diagnostic imaging (for example compression ultrasound) and start treatment per local guidance if imaging will be delayed

distractorRationale.a: Correct: unilateral swelling, warmth and tenderness after major surgery suggest DVT, which needs prompt diagnosis and treatment decisions.
distractorRationale.c: Ignoring the leg risks pulmonary embolism.

questions.explanation: Unilateral calf swelling, warmth and tenderness after major surgery are features of DVT. Prompt imaging and treatment reduce the risk of pulmonary embolism; the choice of anticoagulant and dose must follow current NICE, BNF and local guidance.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man is on day 7 after an open abdominal operation. A nurse reports a pink watery discharge from the midline wound that has soaked the dressing and a small area of the wound that looks open. He has a mild fever. Explain how you would assess and manage the wound complications you are considering, and when you would escalate. Include thromboembolic risk in your answer.
markingGuide: Recognise pink serous discharge as a possible sign of impending fascial dehiscence, as well as surgical site infection
Assess ABCDE, examine the wound in good light with sterile technique, check for erythema, collection, pus and the depth of any gap, and whether bowel is visible
If dehiscence or evisceration is suspected: cover with saline-soaked gauze, keep nil by mouth, secure intravenous access, call the senior surgeon and prepare for theatre; give analgesia
If infection: swab, consider opening the wound if there is a collection, and give antibiotics according to local guidance and microbiology results
Look for risk factors (diabetes, obesity, malnutrition, smoking, steroids, coughing, poor wound closure) and optimise
Consider thromboembolism: assess for unilateral leg swelling or breathlessness, review prophylaxis and mobilisation, and investigate promptly if suspected
Escalate early to the registrar and document findings and plan
questions.explanation: A good answer distinguishes infection from dehiscence, describes the first-aid steps for evisceration, and includes escalation and thromboembolic assessment. Antibiotic choices and doses must be checked against current guidance.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old woman is on day 2 after an open cholecystectomy. She has a distended abdomen, nausea and vomiting, and has not passed flatus. Describe a structured assessment of the distension, including the differential diagnosis, the examination, the investigations and the initial management.
markingGuide: Immediate: ABCDE, vital signs, review the trend, intravenous access and early senior involvement if unwell
History: pain character, vomiting, flatus and bowel opening, analgesia including opioids, fluid intake and urine output, previous surgery or hernia
Differential: ileus, mechanical obstruction (adhesion, internal hernia), anastomotic or bile leak and peritonitis, urinary retention, haemorrhage or collection, ascites
Examination: inspect, palpate for tenderness, guarding and bladder, percuss (tympanic versus dull), auscultate, check hernial orifices, wound, drains and the rectum
Investigations: urea and electrolytes including potassium and magnesium, FBC, CRP, lactate, bladder scan, and abdominal X-ray or CT according to findings

Initial management: correct electrolytes, minimise opioids, maintenance fluids, antiemetic suited to the cause, nasogastric decompression if vomiting, mobilise, and escalate if peritonism, sepsis or obstruction
questions.explanation: A strong answer is structured, links features to the likely cause and ensures that dangerous diagnoses are excluded. It states clear triggers for escalation.
